overview.description: Polish Bank (also simply known as 'Bank' or the 'Russian' variation) is an intense, high-stakes comparing game purely designed for gambling. It belongs to the same family of games as 'Red Dog' and 'Slippery Sam'. Players bet against a central pool that they hold a higher card of a specific suit than a revealed target. It is known for its strict 'Blind Betting' rules, where touching your cards before wagering is a penalized offense.

history.origins: Likely developed from 18th-century European banking games like 'Pharaon' and 'Basset'. It became widely popular in Eastern Europe and among immigrant communities in the US.
timeline: 1880s: Recorded as a popular gambling game in Polish urban centers.
1920s: Gathers a reputation in Chicago and New York as a high-stakes 'Underground' game.
1970s: Included in Hoyle's collections as a representative for 'Comparative Banking'.
Present: Occasionally played in informal settings and localized gambling circles.
history.evolution: The game was designed to be much faster than Poker, with immediate payouts and a rotating dealer ('The Bank') to ensure fairness in a casual setting.
history.cultural: The 'No-Touch' rule adds a layer of psychological pressure and prevents cheating by swapping cards from a sleeve.

setup.players: Four to seven players; five or six is ideal for pace and pool size (Bank requires a banker plus punters).
setup.deck: Standard 52-card deck of French playing cards; ace is high and two is low. One pack per round.
setup.dealing: The dealer (Banker) deals three cards face-down to each player and themselves.

rules.objective: Win chips from the pool by matching the suit of the target card with a higher-ranking card from your hand.
rules.gameplay: Each player contributes a stake to the pool. The dealer gives three cards face-down to each player and turns up one card; if it is not lower than an eight (ace lowest), the dealer continues turning up cards until such a card is exposed. The player on the dealer's left, without touching or looking at their three cards, may bet the amount of the pool or any part of it that they hold a card of the same suit higher than the turn-up. If they win they take that amount from the pool; if they lose they pay it to the pool. Each player does the same in turn, the dealer last. When the pool is exhausted a fresh stake is put in. After a round the deal passes. No player may touch any cards until making a bet; the penalty is a fine to the pool of twice the stake and loss of the right to bet that round.
keyRules: Blind bet: do not look at or touch your three cards before announcing your bet.
Bet up to the full pool or any part of it that you hold a same-suit higher card than the turn-up.
Turn-up must be lower than 8 (ace low); dealer keeps turning until it is.
Touching cards before betting: fine of twice the stake to the pool and loss of bet right for that round.

strategy.basic: Bet the minimum when the target card is high (e.g., a 7). Since you need to beat the card in the SAME SUIT, and 1/4 of your cards are typically the right suit, the odds of having a card higher than a 7 in that specific suit are low. Bet the pool when the target card is a 2 or 3â€”your odds of having *any* higher card of that suit are much better.
strategy.intermediate: Pool Management: If the pool is small, bet more aggressively to 'Empty' it and become the next dealer. If the pool is massive, the pressure is on the Banker. As a player, you only risk what you bet, but the Banker is responsible for the pool's health across many rounds. Watch for 'Suit Clustering'â€”if the previous 5 players all lost on a Spade target, the odds of the remaining deck being 'Spade-Rich' are higher.
strategy.advanced: The 'Blind' Advantage: While the game is mostly luck, the strategy lies in 'Bet Sizing' relative to the Target Card. A pro player treats Polish Bank like a game of 'Dynamic Odds'. Since you have 3 cards, the probability of hitting a specific suit is ~58%. If the target card is a 4, you have a solid edge against the house. Always bet the maximum allowed when the target is 2, 3, or 4.
tips: Keep your hands under the table until your bet is announced to avoid the 'Double Stake' penalty.
If the Banker is winning many rounds in a row, the pool will become too largeâ€”consider a communal 'Cap' on the bank.

difficulty.easy: Bets the maximum on high target cards; ignores the 'No-Touch' penalty; poor bet sizing.
difficulty.medium: Understands 'Target Card' probability; bets larger on 2s/3s; respects the pool size.
difficulty.hard: Expert at 'Suite-Bias' calculation (tracking seen cards); perfectly optimizes bet size for max ROI; never triggers the penalty.

engine.handRankingSystem: Single-card comparison: same suit, higher rank beats the turn-up.
engine.deckDescription: A standard 52-card French deck; no jokers. Polish Bank is a gambling game: players bet against the bank; cards are dealt and compared or played according to the variant; the full deck is used for each round.
engine.suitDescription: The four French suits (hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades) each have thirteen cards. Suit may break ties or determine payouts in the bank game; the exact role depends on the Polish Bank variant.
engine.rankDescription: Standard ranks Ace through King; rank order determines hand value or comparison in the bank game. Point values and payout rules depend on the specific Polish Bank variant being played.
engine.dealPattern: Three cards face-down to each player and to dealer; one card turned up as target. Turn-up must be lower than 8 (ace low); dealer continues turning until such a card is exposed.
